title: Agentive_logic
summary:
Agentive logic refers to formal logical frameworks used to reason about agency, actions, and the capacities of agents. It is closely related to the broader field of modal logic of action in philosophy and computer science.

The study of agentive logic encompasses several major approaches. STIT logic (sees to it that), developed by Nuel Belnap and collaborators, interprets the operator stit_i(phi) as "agent i sees to it that phi." Dynamic logic, originally invented by computer scientists to analyze computer action, provides another framework where actions are directly studied as part of the ontology. BDI (Belief-Desire-Intention) logic, formalized by Rao and Georgeff, uses branching-time temporal logic with modal operators for Belief, Goal, and Intention.

John Maier proposed a general account of what he calls "the agentive modalities," taking as its primitive the decision-theoretic notion of an option. This account relates to the standard semantics for "can" and to positions in the free will debates. Segerberg's Outline of a Logic of Action attempts to reconcile the stit view of agency with the dynamic logic view of event types, giving formal representations of agentive concepts such as "the agent is about to do alpha" as well as deontic concepts such as "it is obligatory for the agent to do alpha."

Agentive logic has applications in multi-agent systems, game theory, normative reasoning, and artificial intelligence. The interaction between game theory and modal logic is a flourishing area of research, with applications to understanding cooperation and competition among agents as information available to them evolves. Key references include Belnap, Perloff and Xu's Facing the Future: Agents and Choices in Our Indeterminist World (2001), and entries in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy on the Logic of Action and Modal Logic.
